analysis.one_liner: Limits how much credit card debt lenders can extend to college students without a parent cosigning.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap credit offered to college students was referred to a House committee and never received a vote, dying at the end of the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal lending law so credit card companies could not give a full-time college student under 21 a credit limit above a small share of the student's own income unless a parent, guardian, or spouse cosigned. It would also have required lenders to verify a student's income before opening an account, required written parental approval to raise limits on cosigned accounts, and barred issuing multiple cards to incomeless students who already had one from the same company. The idea was to stop lenders from signing up students who had no way to repay and then pursuing parents for the debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Full-time traditional-aged college students and their parents. Students would be protected from credit limits far beyond their ability to repay, and parents who cosign would gain control over limit increases. Students with no verifiable income could no longer stack multiple cards from the same lender.

how_it_helps.text: It caps the credit any one lender could extend to a full-time student under 21 at the greater of 20% of the student's annual income or $500, and total limits across all cards at 30% of income, unless a parent or guardian cosigns.

It requires written approval from a cosigning parent before a credit limit can be raised on a student's account, and requires lenders to verify a student's income and credit history before opening an account.
It bars issuing a second card to a student with no verifiable income who already holds one with the same lender or its affiliate.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which would lose the ability to extend unsecured credit to students without income and to collect from parents on debts students could not pay. Some students without a willing cosigner would have had less access to credit.

drawbacks.text: Credit limits tied to a student's own income could have kept cards out of the hands of low-income students who might responsibly use small lines of credit to build a credit history.
Requiring a parent, guardian, or spouse to cosign pushes the risk onto families, and students without a willing or creditworthy cosigner would have had a harder time getting a first card.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—less debt for students and fewer surprise bills for parents—was real but targeted at a narrow, well-documented harm. The cost is that some young adults without parental support would have found credit harder to get, since cosigning or income proof would be required. The bigger weakness was political: it died without even a committee vote, so its merits were never weighed on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without any vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 2, 2007 and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
On September 5, 2007 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and no further action followed.
No vote was ever taken in the House or Senate, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers kept unrestricted ability to market cards to students; students and parents gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Louise Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Credit card industry
against.role: Credit card issuers and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on student card marketing and underwriting during the period when Congress considered, and ultimately did not pass, standalone student-card limits before the broader CARD Act was enacted in 2009.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with 11 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsor, and it never advanced far enough for a recorded vote that would show the parties' positions.

industries.note: The bill would have limited how much credit card debt lenders could extend to students without parental cosigning or verified income, cutting off a profitable market segment that often carries high balances and fees. It never took effect.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities with card-marketing partnerships
industries.note: Lenders market cards on campus partly through arrangements with schools; stricter underwriting would have reduced the volume of student accounts opened through those channels.
